en: The Sūtra on the Grounds of Practice of the Devaputra Maheśvara,
translated by the Tripitaka Master Śīladharma, Dharma-Master and Acting Assistant Director of the Court of State Ceremonial,
Grand Officer of the Third Rank, under Imperial Decree during the Western Heavens (India).
Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

At that time, during the mealtime, the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana put on his robes, took up his bowl, and by the power of his diligence, exercised great supernormal powers, emitting countless rays of light; those rays were golden in color and illuminated the entirety of space.

Furthermore, by means of his supernormal powers, he transformed his body—making it sometimes large and sometimes small, sometimes one and sometimes many—like a flame of fire, and proceeded to Mount Kunlun.

The mountain peaks were like snow; within those summits, the ground was adorned with various jewels such as gold, silver, lapis lazuli, pearls, agate, coral, and mani-gems, and there were palaces exquisitely decorated with every kind of rare treasure.

In the midst of it is the palace of Maheśvara, two yojanas wide and five yojanas high, brilliantly illuminated. Sixty great deities constantly guard it, while hundreds of thousands of celestial maidens surround its four sides, performing the seven kinds of musical entertainment.
In the four directions of the palace, there are seven halls, each one krośa in width, all adorned with the seven precious gems.
Furthermore, on each of the four sides, there is a bathing pool, filled to the brim with pure and clear water of ambrosia.
In that pond, white lotuses and kumuda lilies bloom like the white moon of heaven, adorned above with gold, silver, and mani jewels.
There, the Great Lord Mahādeva and Queen Umā sit together upon a lion throne, while the hosts of devas constantly come to surround them, paying homage and making offerings.
That deva suddenly heard the sound of lute music, its tones subtle and exquisite; having heard it, he became attached to it, and his mind grew confused and distracted.

At that time, although the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana heard the music, he subdued his mind through the roots of goodness of fearlessness and remained without attachment. Like Mount Sumeru rising from the great ocean, standing firm and unmoving, he practiced the sublime conduct of diligence and received the offerings of all the world’s multitudes. His physical form was dignified and majestic, his deportment was perfect, and he held an alms-bowl in his hand.
When Queen Umā suddenly saw him, doubt arose in her mind, and she addressed the son of heaven, saying:
"Who is this person?

Clad in dharma robes, he is upright, majestic, and serene; his faculties are subdued and his deportment is perfect. His circular light shines brilliantly like the rising sun, and he sits unmoving like Mount Sumeru."
Having heard these words, the deva observed the Venerable One and spoke again:
"O Queen! Is this one your acquaintance?"
The Queen replied,
"I have never seen it before, nor do I know of it now. Maheśvara said:

"This is a disciple of the Buddha, one of great merit who has transcended desire; he is able to destroy all faults and brings peace and happiness to sentient beings through his teaching, and has come here for the sake of alms."
Having heard these words, Queen Umā addressed the Deva, saying:
"What is that teacher like?
What are his physical characteristics?"
"What kind of spiritual power, moral authority, and unprecedented qualities does he possess?
I wish to hear about them.
Śakra devānām indra said:

"The teacher of that person, throughout three incalculable eons, sought great enlightenment and extensively cultivated the power of merit; performing what is difficult to do in this world, he practiced the perfection of giving (*dāna-pāramitā*), bestowing food and drink, clothing, bedding, medicine, gold and silver, precious gems, slaves and servants, vehicles, cities and towns, villages, as well as great treasuries and the rank of king. He also gave his wives, children, sons, and daughters to various brahmins; yet in his heart, there was not even a speck of dust of the affliction of stinginess or attachment, nor was there even the name of craving."

Furthermore, out of compassion for sentient beings, he gave away his head, eyes, marrow, brain, nose, tongue, body, and flesh without even a speck of thought of suffering, nor did he harbor any pretense; practicing true giving, he fulfilled the *dāna-pāramitā* in order to seek the fruit of the great power of Bodhi.

Moreover, throughout three incalculable eons (*asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*), in order to counter various objective appearances (*viṣaya-nimitta*), he practiced the *śīla-pāramitā*, steadfastly observing the prohibitions and precepts, and through the majesty of his ethical discipline, he constantly received offerings from gods and humans.

Again, because of the inequality between enemies and kin, and the emotional discrepancies between the adverse and the favorable, he practiced the *kṣānti-pāramitā*, subduing his mind with the Eightfold Noble Path, and through joyful forbearance, he brought his mind to equanimity.

Furthermore, out of compassion for sentient beings of the three grades—superior, middling, and inferior—and in order to benefit and bring them joy and happiness, he practices the perfection of diligence (*vīrya-pāramitā*), exerting himself with vigor day and night.

Moreover, fearing that his mind might become distracted or regress due to false objects of perception, he practices the perfection of meditation (*dhyāna-pāramitā*), causing the mind to become resolute, tranquil, and pliant.
Furthermore, he brought forth wisdom by reading, reciting, and discerning the subtle and wondrous sūtras, practicing the *prajñāpāramitā*.

Thus, for three incalculable *kalpas*, he practiced the six *pāramitās* while seeking the knowledge of all-knowledge (*sarvajñājñāna*). Now, having attained the perfection of the state of Buddhahood, he has subdued all Māras and realized the principle of *nirvāṇa*. His form and mind are subtle and wondrous; he is endowed with the thirty-two marks and eighty secondary characteristics, adorned with golden radiance and a halo like the sun. Peerless within the triple world, he has emerged from the hardships of saṃsāra into the peace and liberation of *mokṣa*.

When Maheśvara had spoken these words, Queen Umā heard them and was filled with joy once more; having now understood that the great fruits obtained through practices such as giving can be realized, she asked again:
"O Deva, what specific karmic actions did you cultivate in your previous lives?"
"I pray that you will grant me joy and briefly explain it for my sake.
Then Maheśvara spoke again, saying:
"Listen attentively now; I shall explain it for you."
"O Queen of Heaven!

Throughout countless koṭis of kalpas in the past, I practiced giving, made offerings, cultivated merit, observed the precepts, and perfumed my wisdom under the Great Muni Buddha. Since that time, I have obtained the retribution of mastery, attaining eight kinds of sovereignty within eight successive births."

Throughout my successive lives, I have practiced generosity, observed the precepts, and engaged in asceticism, seeking mastery and sovereignty, the liberation of sensual desires, and even ultimate quiescence; the same was true for my pursuit of peace and happiness. Therefore, I have practiced generosity, the discernment of wisdom, and the one-pointed guarding of the mind without interruption.
Having spoken these words, Maheśvara, within his own palace, filled a golden bowl with a hundred flavors of exquisite fragrant rice and approached Maudgalyāyana to offer it with a sincere heart.
Venerable Maudgalyāyana accepted the bowl of rice and rose into the air, intending to return.
Mahādeva, possessing the knowledge of past lives, addressed Maudgalyāyana, saying:
"Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana!
Stay for a moment now and listen attentively to my words.
Only after an exceedingly long time does a Buddha appear in the world.
I recall that in a past life, I was the sovereign of this great earth; I could bring forth and destroy the world, serving as the teacher of the three realms, and there was no one who equaled me.
"Listen to these words and go with a single-minded focus to that Mount Gandhamādana.
Thereupon, Mahāmaudgalyāyana exercised his supernormal powers and soared through the air to Mount Gandhamādana.
On one side of that mountain was a sacred pool named Heavenly Water; he bathed therein.

Having finished his bath, he sat upon Mount Fragrant Intoxication and opened his golden bowl; the rice within was exquisite, endowed with perfect color and fragrance, and transformed into celestial food.
After Maudgalyāyana had finished eating, a celestial maiden suddenly presented him with pure water.
Having accepted it, he purified his five limbs and sat upon that mountain, fixing his mind and entering meditative concentration (*samādhi*). He engaged in contemplative reflection, thinking:
"The Lord of the *Īśvara* heavens said:"
"A Buddha appears only after an exceedingly long period of time.

This cannot be known even after passing through a thousand births; it cannot be known even within hundreds of thousands of births; nor can it be known even after passing through hundreds of thousands of koṭis of births.
Rising from meditative concentration, he went to Mount Mahendra and entered into contemplation, yet he could not know [the answer].
He then entered a cave on Mount Mahendra, the king of mountains, and entered into contemplation, yet he still could not know it.
From there, he traveled throughout seventy mountains, engaging in meditation and reflection, but he was unable to know it in any of them.
Furthermore, he went to the thirty-two continents and sat in silent contemplation, yet he still could not know it.
Maudgalyāyana said:
"The words and intentions arising from the wisdom of that Mahāmaheśvara are such that even the lesser śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas are unable to know them."
Then, with single-minded focus, he addressed the Elder Śāriputra:
"Venerable One!
Listen attentively!"
"On the summit of Mount Kailāsa, I beheld Maheśvara, who spoke to me, saying:
'Only after an exceedingly long period of time will a Buddha appear in the world.
To this meaning, I can ultimately find no understanding."

"Venerable sir, you now possess great wisdom and have profoundly discerned the subtle and the minute; you know the number of drops of rain that have fallen over three years and three months, you know the number of droplets in the waters of the four great oceans, and you know the mental activities of the people of the four great continents."
"Such great wisdom possessed by these sons of the Buddha should be understood through the meaning of these words; I only pray that, out of compassion, you will briefly reveal it for us.

At that time, having heard these words, the Elder Śāriputra immediately entered meditative absorption and contemplated this matter for hundreds of thousands of koṭis of lifetimes, yet he was unable to understand it.
At that time, the Elder Mahākāśyapa said to Śāriputra:
"The Dharma spoken by Maheśvara is of profound intent; it is subtle and difficult to fathom."
"If you were to obtain the power of that Buddha, only then would you understand;
if you were to contemplate with your own power, it would be like holding a blade of grass and attempting to measure Mount Sumeru.
At that time, Mahākāśyapa thought to himself:

"If, in the interval between a single thought-moment or an instant, one were to behold events of the distant past as clearly as if they were in the palm of one's hand, only the Great Wisdom of a Buddha could know such things."
Then Mahākāśyapa, emitting a stainless and pure voice, addressed Mahāmaudgalyāyana, saying:

"If Mahāmaheśvara were to manifest his own conduct and practices, no one in the human or celestial realms would be able to understand them; only the peerless wisdom of omniscience within the three realms can realize and know them."

Why is this? It is because the Buddha, the World-Honored One, throughout worlds as numerous as the sands of hundreds of thousands of koṭis of Ganges Rivers, fully understands all past and present sentient beings—their superior, middling, and inferior faculties, their dispositions, and their mental activities—as clearly as if looking into the palm of his hand; this is what is called the "knowledge of all modes" (sarvajñajñāna).

At that time, the elders Mahāmaudgalyāyana, Śāriputra, and Mahākāśyapa went together to where the Buddha was. They circumambulated the World-Honored One, prostrated themselves with their five limbs touching the ground, paid homage with single-minded devotion, and withdrew to sit at one side.
At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing their thoughts, looked upon them with a smile.
Then Mahāmaudgalyāyana praised the Buddha’s merits: “The Buddha’s face is as dignified and beautiful as a blooming golden lotus;

his compassionate countenance is serene and joyful, and his marks of fortune are profound. His teeth are even and closely set, and his body is most exquisite. He emits great radiance—blue, yellow, red, and white—which shines universally throughout the world, so that mountains, rivers, and deep valleys are all made bright. Even if hundreds of thousands of koṭis of suns and moons were gathered together, their light could not equal it. He proclaims the flavor of the Dharma of coolness, which universally moistens the three realms; there are no sentient beings who do not receive its benefit.”
Having praised him thus, he paid homage with reverence and said:
"World-Honored One!
On one occasion, I took my alms-bowl and went to the palace of Maheśvara to beg for food there."
At that time, Maheśvara saw me holding my alms bowl and receiving food according to the Dharma, and he said to me:
"It will be after an exceedingly long period of time before a Buddha finally appears."
"I have never been able to fully comprehend these words.

The Buddha possesses all-encompassing wisdom; He clearly knows the various mental activities of sentient beings throughout all the nayuta-koṭi Ganges-sand worlds in the universe, as clearly as if looking into the palm of His hand. His tongue is broad and long, extending so far as to cover His face. I only pray that the Muni will resolve my doubts."
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Mahāmaudgalyāyana with a subtle and sublime Brahma-voice:
“Listen attentively now and reflect upon it well!
I shall analyze and explain it for you.”
In the past, eighty-four thousand kalpas ago, there appeared in the world a Buddha, a Samyaksaṃbuddha, named Guṇasāgara.
There was a great city also named Guṇasāgara; in it lived a brahmin named Śānta, who had two sons—one named Śaṅkha and the other named Ruci—who gradually grew up to be intelligent and highly wise.
Both being weary of birth and death, they paid homage to their parents and said to their father:
"We wish to enter the mountains to practice the Way there.
Their parents did not grant permission.
"You must not go," [his father said].
He replied to his father again, saying,
"I must go to practice the Way."
Having spoken thus three times, he departed from his parents and entered the mountain valleys, dwelling in a grass hut among the mountains.
Ten paces outside the hut lived an elderly brahmin practicing the methods of a rishi, and there was also another person living nearby who practiced his own discipline.
Once, on a festival day, the four of them gathered together and asked one another about the matters they each delighted in and sought.
Ruci asked the old Brahmin, saying:
"What practice do you cultivate, and what fruit or reward do you seek?"
The old brahmin said,
"That which I practice seeks the body of Brahmā and a lifespan of a thousand years in the heavens.
He then asked a neighboring practitioner:
"What practice do you cultivate, and what fruit or retribution do you seek?
He replied of his own accord:
"I seek to become the lord of the three realms and live for a thousand years in heaven."
The great seer Śaṅkha declared of himself:
"I seek a thousand years in heaven and the love and respect of the world.
The seer Ruci, possessed of great wisdom, addressed him, saying:

"You three have sought and attained the worldly fruits of accomplishment; what I now seek is for the sake of those sentient beings in saṃsāra—whether of the world with form or without form, two-legged, four-legged, many-legged, or legless, and whether superior, middling, or inferior—to bring them all to liberation."

"Thus, at a later time, the Buddha was followed and surrounded by countless hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayas of Śakras, Brahmās, humans, devas, and the multitudes of both ordinary and holy beings from the heavens."

That Buddha sat upon a seat of golden lotus; his body was clad in crimson robes and his face was like the full moon. He emitted auspicious light in blue, yellow, red, and white, descending upon the great earth to illuminate all sentient beings and cause their minds to become pure.
The four practitioners who had been there previously approached the Buddha.
At that time, the old brahmin offered white *śirīṣa* flowers to the Buddha, prostrated, circumambulated him, and made this aspiration:
"By this merit of mine, may I become the Lord of the Brahma World, with five faces and a majestic countenance, fulfilling the aspirations of countless sentient beings."
Next, one seer offered a piece of iron to the Buddha and further anointed the Buddha’s feet with fragrant oil, making this aspiration:
"By this merit of mine, may I attain the body of Nārāyaṇa and become the sovereign of the three realms."
Next, the ṛṣi Śaṅkha lit three lamps and offered three needles, making his offering with a sincere heart and uttering this vow:

"By offering these three lamps and three needles, may I be endowed with the three eyes and obtain the trident; in every successive birth, may I constantly practice giving and fulfill my vows, becoming a sovereign of the world who attains the eight masteries, and may my desires be fulfilled and my mind and intellect be sharp."
At that time, Ruci’s topknot was exquisite; his hair was long and red. He then untied his topknot and spread it upon the road, addressing the World-Honored One:

“I pray that the Buddha, out of compassion, will step over my hair. The two feet of the Buddha have attained what has never been seen before within the three realms: they possess the thousand-spoked wheel with webbed membranes, and the marks of the banner, the pennant, and the vajra—such seal-marks as these, their patterns like fine embroidery, wondrously and excellently adorned!”
The Buddha then stepped over it and made this vow:
"By virtue of this merit of mine, may I attain Buddhahood and rescue all sentient beings wandering in saṃsāra."

"Thus, after these four individuals had each made their vows, that old Brahmin, through the various merits he had cultivated, attained the body of a Brahmā King. He possessed five heads and faces and became the lord of the three realms; because he had offered auspicious flowers as a gift, he was moved by this karma to hold a celestial fly-whisk in his hand."

If a practitioner cultivates this next stage, the roots of goodness they cultivate will yield boundless merit; they shall obtain the body of Nārāyaṇa, and through the offering of iron, they will be moved by the reward of holding the Cakra-ratna (Wheel Treasure) called "Wondrous Manifestation," which is capable of destroying all asuras.

The third was the Ṛṣi Śaṅkha: by offering three lamps, he caused three eyes to appear on his face; by offering three needles, he obtained a trident; and by circumambulating the World-Honored One, he attained the eight kinds of sovereignty cherished by the world, becoming its sovereign and able to bring about the creation and destruction of the world.

As for the fourth, Lu-zhi (Ruci), by virtue of his vow when he made an offering of his hair, he shall transcend desire and pass beyond the three realms, attain the wisdom of all-knowledge, and be titled the God among Gods.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to reiterate this meaning, spoke in verse:
"Having offered the most supreme and auspicious flowers and circumambulated [the Buddha] again,
one shall attain the body of a Brahmā King and be called the Lord of Sahā."
Adorned with five faces, holding a celestial whisk;
by giving iron, one gains merit and becomes the deity Nārāyaṇa,
who holds a wondrously manifest wheel and is able to destroy the asuras.
He lit those three lamps and offered them with three needles;
consequently, his face manifested three eyes and his hand held a trident.
The great seer Ruci made an offering by spreading out his hair.
By means of these sublime and virtuous causes, they shall attain the fruit of Buddhahood.
The Lord of the Vaśavartin Heaven recalled that throughout incalculable kalpas of the past,
through those causes of their practice, they shall subsequently become Buddhas.
"Appearing in the world, it cannot be known by śrāvakas;
only the Buddha, the Unsurpassed Awakened One, understands and can discern it.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Maudgalyāyana, saying:
“The body born of that Maheśvara is truly most rare.
When he descended from the Brahma Heaven to the human realm, there was a female hungry ghost in the Cold Forest named Māyā; he united with her, and she immediately became pregnant.”
He was then conceived within the womb of a female ghost; subsequently, he took birth with three eyes on his face and a radiance upon his body.
When his mother saw him, she fled in terror; however, by virtue of his merit, the light illuminated all the hosts of ghosts in the Śītavana cemetery.
At that time, the host of spirits saw the light like the sun; their hearts were filled with doubt and fear, and they immediately asked:
"Who are you? He then replied:
"I am Maheśvara, named Svayambhū.
When the host of spirits heard this, they paid homage with reverence and praised him, saying:
"Your power and diligence are supreme; your physical form is most exquisite."
Furthermore, devas and Brahmas alike came together to gaze upon him.

When the assembly of devas and humans saw that among the five heads of that Brahmā, one was hideous, they were filled with alarm and fear, and their minds were tormented by distress. They said to Maheśvara:
"Could you please cut off that head for us?"
Maheśvara addressed the host of devas, saying:
"If you were to cut off his head, I would incur the sin of killing Brahmā.
The host of devas spoke again:
"If there be any transgressions or offenses, we shall share in them.
Then Maheśvara granted his consent, saying, "So be it."
He immediately transformed himself into the body of a great hawk and plucked off one head with his talons.
Therefore, Mahādeva held the head of Brahmā in his hand, as was known universally by all the devas and the assembly of brahmins.
When the Buddha had spoken these words, the Elder Mahāmaudgalyāyana and the others listened with single-minded devotion and were all greatly rejoiced.
This concludes the *Buddhabhāṣita-maheśvaradeva-pūrvabhūmi-sūtra*.
